items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 14 February, the Government w ill look to progress the Address in Reply
debate and conclude members’ maiden speech es. A number of bills on the Order Paper
will receive their first reading. By agreemen t of the Business Committee of the House,
the House will take extended sitting hours on Thursday, 16 February. This is to progress
a number of Treaty settlement bills and Statutes Amendment bills Nos 2 and 3, which
have the broad support of the House.
Fishing Industry—Set-net Ban
1. GARETH HUGHES (Green)  to the Minister for Primary Industries : Will he
extend the Taranaki set net ban after the rece nt death of a Maui’s dolphin in a fishing
net?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: The Ministry of
Agriculture and Forestry and the Department of Conservati on are currently working on
a M āui’s dolphin recovery plan. I will wait until that plan has been presented before
making any decisions on set-net bans in Tara naki. I have certainly asked for that work
to be done as quickly as possible.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Can the Minister guarantee that no M āui’s dolphins will die while
that recovery plan is being carried out?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Will the Minister take responsibility for the recent M āui’s dolphin
death, given that research published by the Mi nistry of Fisheries in 2005 established
that Māui’s dolphins swim in the area where the dolphin died?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: No, I will not take responsibility for this death. It is my
understanding that when the current set-ne t ban was established, it was covering the
area where Māui’s dolphins were thought to swim. My information is that this is an area
where they previously had not found Māui’s dolphins, and that is why we will await the
recovery plan before we make further decisions on that ban.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Will the Minister take responsibility for the recent M āui’s dolphin
death, given his Government’s inaction fo llowing a submission in 2009 including video
footage of a Māui’s dolphin swimming in the vicinity in unprotected Taranaki waters?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: This Government and the former Government have taken
action. The set-net ban was put in place in 2008 by the Hon Jim Anderton. It was
subsequently challenged in court, requiring the then Minister, the Hon Phil Heatley, to
further review the information and to stick with the extended set-net ban.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Given a Ministry of Fisheries report, video footage submitted to the
Government, and now a dead dolphin, what more evidence does the Government need
that dolphins swim in thes e unprotected Taranaki waters for him to act with an
extension of the set-net ban?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I have given the member the answer to that question. The
information I now want is the completion of the M āui’s dolphin recovery plan. When I
get that information, I will further consider that report.
256 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Given that M āui’s dolphins will become extinct if mortality
exceeds just one individual over 5 to 7 years, and that we have had two M āui’s dolphin
deaths in the last 5 months, why will the Minister not use his powers under the Fisheries
Act and put a moratorium on set-net fishing while more research is being carried out?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I certainly accept that this is a species under extreme threat
of extinction. Set-net banning—and the infl uence of human interaction—is but one
factor in the death of these dolphins. I will work with th e Ministry of Agriculture and
Forestry, I will work with the Department of Conservation, and I will await the report of
the recovery plan before making further decisions.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Given the Minister’s inabil ity to guarantee that more M āui’s
dolphins will not die on his watch and his refusal to implement greater protection
measures now, is he prepared to be an accessory to extinction?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: This is a relatively small population. It is an endangered
species, but there are a number of reasons why this extinction could be caused, of which
human interaction is but one.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: I seek leave to tabl e this DVD containing a 31-second video shot
by Taranaki fisherman Ray O’Donnell of a M āui’s dolphin in the area where the
Government alleges Māui’s dolphins do not travel in Taranaki.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection. I remind members that points of order should be heard in silence.
DVD, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Trade—China Strategy
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What actions is the Government ta king to boost economic linkages with
China?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Last Friday I
attended the launch by the Prime Minister of  the China Strategy, which provides a clear
direction for Government action over the next 5 years and aims to double two-way trade
with China, from $10 billion to $20 bill ion, by 2015. Our efforts will focus on sectors
with scale and growth capac ity: food and beverage, agri business, information and
communications technology, and high-value manufacturing, togeth er with growing
services in tourism and international education. Some examples of how we will achieve
this include working with exporters on how to  do business in China, facilitating more
direct links to China, and negotiation of a fisheries and aquaculture arrangement.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How does the Government’s actions in China fit into its broader
economic development strategy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: In order to provide long-term, sustainable jobs and
competitive industries, businesses must be ab le to access customers and markets, and
this is where the Government can assist. In  fact, it is one of th e six key drivers of
business growth we are focused on. China is the second strategy to be launched
following the launch of the India Strategy last October. In addition to India and China,
other strategies under deve lopment include the US, Aust ralia, South-east Asia, the
Middle East, and the European Union.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Do the Government’s attempts to boost economic linkages
with China include a representative of th e Chinese Government making representations
to the New Zealand Government on Ch inese businesses buying productive New
Zealand land?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not aware of any such representations.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How important is China to New Zealand’s economy?
9 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 257

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is very important. China is, in fact, our second-biggest
trading partner now, and of course Australia is our largest trading partner.
Coincidentally, Australia has China as its largest trading partne r. The current global
economic uncertainty has only reinforced the importance of China to this country. That
is why the attitude of the Opposition parties is hard to understand. They claim they want
more jobs and better wages—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question was from the member’s own colleague and I
do not think we need to get into Opposition parties on those grounds.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that the actions of the Government in
relation to China include the dispatching of Christchurch Mayor Bob Parker there?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the Mayor of Christchurch went under his own
steam.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If a representative of the Chinese Government did make
representations to the New Zealand G overnment on Chinese businesses buying
productive New Zealand land, would he be expected to know about it?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, not specifically, and I would remind the member that
countries and members of countries make representations to Ministers all the time about
all sorts of things.
Electoral Broadcasting—Prime Minister’s Radio Live Show
3. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
Does he stand by his statement that his hour -long show on Radio Live on 30 September
2011 was an “election free zone”?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery) on
behalf of the Prime Minister: Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Did he or his office seek or receive advice from the Electoral
Commission on whether the “hour with the PM” show could breach electoral
broadcasting law; if so, what did that advice say?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am informed the Prime Minister’s office discussed
the matter with the broadcaster. Radio Live , I understand, then s ought advice from the
Electoral Commission. After r eceiving that advice, Radio Live decided to go forward
with the programme.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Will the Prime Minister be declaring the value of an hour of free
radio time as a donation, as required under the Electoral Act?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Prime Minister has no obligations under the
Electoral Act.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has the Prime Minister received a ny advice as to the value of an
hour’s air time on Radio Live, and was this re flected in the declaration of donations for
that period?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am unable to answer that question at this point.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If the show was an election-free zone, as the Prime Minister has
said, and he was not there for the purpose of  getting electoral advantage for himself and
the National Party, what reason did he actually have for hosting the show?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands,
millions of New Zealanders find everything he says just fascinating.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Has he or his office sought advice as to whether he has abetted a
crime under section 66 of the Crimes Act by hosting the “hour with the PM” on Radio
Live?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: This matter is currently referred to the police. The
police are investigating Radio Live in this matter.

Health Targets—Changes
4. Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua)  to the Minister of Health : What
improvements, if any, have been made to the Government’s national health targets?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Preventive health is very important to
this Government, and that is why we are lif ting health targets in this vital area. For
example, in the area of immunisation, the target is moving from 2-year-olds to 8-month-
olds, and this is important because we will ensure more infants are protected from
infectious diseases like measles, whooping cough, and pneumoccocal disease. When we
came to office, only over 70 percent of 2-year-olds were immunised—just over 70
percent. Now 92 percent of 2-year-olds are fully immunised, with virtually no
difference between the rates for M āori, Pacific, and general New Zealanders. We have
also announced the new target for more hear t and diabetes checks, which will be very
important for preventing, detecting, and managing heart disease and diabetes.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: What other improvements are being made to deliver shorter
waits for cancer treatment?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government has announced that we are strengthening the
cancer waiting times target by including chem otherapy in the shorte r waits target, and
on 1 July 2012 all cancer patients ready for radiation or chemotherapy treatment should
begin that treatment within the world gold st andard of 4 weeks. Just a few years ago,
people had to travel to Aust ralia for vital radiation treat ment, and no one has had to do
this since late 2008.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: If the Minister considers preven tion a useful part of improving
New Zealanders’ health and achieving these he alth targets, how will the prevention of
obesity and all its contingent  diseases be achieved, give n the fact that nutrition and
physical exercise programmes such as Healthy Eating - Healthy Action and Mission-On
have been axed?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Well, actually, the Governme nt is spending many, many
millions of dollars promoting healthy eating and healthy action. We certainly have got a
huge investment, particularly in the Ki wisport programme, championed by the Prime
Minister, where $20 million is going in to help schools make young people more active.
Our young people today are far less active than th ey were 20 years ago, and that is why
the Kiwisport investment is so important for dealing with that.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: So if the Minister does consider prevention a useful part of
achieving health targets, what preventive measures is he promoting to address the health
effects of increasing inequality, as described in the New Zealand Herald today?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think the Government is making huge progress in improving
the standard of health care for all New Z ealanders. New Zealand’s levels of rheumatic
fever were at scandalous Third World leve ls under the previous Labour Government.
Annette King made it a health priority in 2001, and then did absolutely nothing about it.
This Government is investing $24 million over 3 years in a programme to stamp out
rheumatic fever, a Third Worl d disease that that party opp osite talked about and did
absolutely nothing about.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: Why is the Government lifti ng performance in the health
targets?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: That is a very good question. The national health targets drive
improved public services right across th e health system. You cannot speed up an
emergency department without improving th e way that a whole hospital runs, with
quicker access to X-rays, to magnetic resonance imaging scans, to CT scans, to a bed, or
to surgery. You cannot immunise more kids if you have not got primary care working
well, and you cannot provide more heart and diabetes checks if hospitals and primary
9 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 259
care are not working together. That is the su ccess of the national health targets—it is
driving whole-of-systems performance improvement.
Christchurch, Recovery—Potential for Rates Increase or Sale of Council Assets
5. Hon LIANNE DALZIEL (Labour—Christchurch East)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
items.text: Did he discuss with the Christchurch City Mayor
reported claims that there had been overtur es from within The Treasury that there was
scope for the city’s rates to be  increased or for assets to be sold to pay for the quake
recovery, and that this c ould be done under the Canterbur y Earthquake Recovery Act
before he called him a clown; if not, why not?
No.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Has he been briefed about what Treasury officials said to the
mayor; if not, why did he describe the ma yor’s quoted statements as an outrageous
abdication of his responsibilities and ca ll him a clown, when he does not know what
was said?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: In the days leading up to that particular injudicious
comment from me there were numerous  discussions going on with the council—
between the senior executives, the mayor, me, and the senior executives of the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority—over a number of issues that we want the
council to take some responsibility, alongsid e us, for. Although Treasury officials will
have talked to the council, I am unaware of exactly what that discussion would have
been about. But let me tell you that when the Government is spending $5.5 billion
anywhere we expect the recipients of th at to have some plan for how they will
participate in what will be a very, very expensive recovery, and that plan has to be a lot
better than saying “We’re just going to put up the rates, and we’re going to borrow a lot
more money.”

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: When he told the media that section 48(3) of the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Act said that the Minister “must not direct any council to (a) set a
rate under section 23 of the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002;”, was he
acknowledging that the Act could be used to  force the council and its holding company
to sell all or any of its assets, and expl aining why the Government voted against our
amendment to the legislation when it was going through the House?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, and any analysis that would suggest that that is
possible is extremely bodgie.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Can he give a guarantee that th e Government will not require
Christchurch City Council to sell any of its assets to help pay for the recovery?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I cannot bind the Christchurch City Council to what it
may decide to do.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very
clear, which was “… that the Government will not require Christchurch City …”. It was
a question of whether the Government would not require it, and he has not dealt with
that question at all.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept that was exactly what the member’s question was.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The member herself has pointed out that capacity for
that does not exist under the Canterbury Ea rthquake Recovery Act,  and therefore it
would have to be a decision by the Christchurch City Council.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was: “Can he
give a guarantee that the Government will not require”—
260 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion I think the Minister did answer, because in his
answer he claimed that the legislation does not give the Government  power to do that.
So he is basically saying no.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Can he give a guarantee, as Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery, that ne ither he nor any member of  the Cabinet committee on
Canterbury earthquake recovery, which he chai rs, has sought or is seeking any external
advice on Christchurch’s assets to assess the potential for their sale to help pay for the
recovery?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Speaking to the very specifics of that question, we
have asked Treasury, obviously, to give us advice about what the capacity is for
Christchurch’s rating base to take on some of the extraordinary expense they have to
face in the future. The list is long: a conve ntion centre, a town hall, a new stadium,
Centennial Pool in the centre of the cit y, the QEII complex, the central city library,
parking buildings throughout the city, a nd many service centres, which are all
destroyed. That is before you even start ta lking about some of the parks and other
recreational facilities that the council has. It is  a billion dollar - plus bill that it has to
face, and we are very interested, given th at we are putting up $5.5 billion, as to how it
might meet that cost.
Local Authorities—Increase in Council Debt Since 2002
6. JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki)  to the Minister of Local Government :
What reports has he received on increases in local government c ouncil debt since the
Local Government Act 2002 was enacted?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The local authority
financial reports show that council debt has quadrupled from $2 billion in 2002 to over
$8 billion today. The increase in debt is sign ificantly greater than any other sector, and
is noted by local government analyst Larry Mitchell to be the N o. 1 issue facing that
sector.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Has local government borrowing slowed in response to the global debt
crisis, in the same way that households and businesses have become cautious of debt?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, household debt grew sh arply between 2000 and 2008,
but stabilised in 2009 and has reduced in 2010 and 2011. Farm debt has also responded
prudently to the global financial crisis and not increased since 2008. In contrast, council
debt has been growing at a faster rate—$500 million of borrowing in 2007, $800
million in 2008, $1,100 million in 2009, a nd $1,800 million in 2010. This ongoing
increase in local government debt is not sustainable.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Why is this increase in debt a concern?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There are three concerns. The fi rst is that c ouncil debt is
actually just rates deferred. The greater the de bt, the less opportunity there is in future
for containing the cost of rates for house holds and businesses. Secondly, council debt
contributes to New Zealand’ s overall indebtedness. Hous eholds and businesses are
doing their bit by pulling back their borrowi ng, and local government needs also to
tighten its belt. My third concern is that fo r some councils their le vel of debt-servicing
costs is becoming so great that it puts the financial viability of their council at risk.
Minimum Wage Review—Minister’s Statements on Increase
7. DARIEN FENTON (Labour) to the Minister of Labour: Does she stand by her
statement that the new minimum wage announ ced yesterday “strikes  the right balance
between protecting low paid workers and ensuring that jobs are not lost.”?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Yes.
9 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 261

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: How is the balance right wh en New Zealand’s top 48 chief
executive officers received an aver age pay increase of $202,000 in 2010, while
thousands of Kiwis on the minimum wage received a pay increase of just 19c an hour in
real terms over the past 4 years under her watch?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: As the member knows, the annual task of setting the
minimum wage is always a balancing act. It  has been a dilemma for many Ministers of
Labour. We set it at the rate that we t hought was the most sustainable to protect
employees’ purchasing power, whilst not jeopard ising jobs and resulting in job losses.
Had we increased it to $15 per hour, our advice was that this could have resulted in the
loss of up to 5,500 jobs. We were not prep ared to actually je opardise those jobs,
because our commitment is to job protection, not job destruction.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Why does she continue to insist  that there will be job losses in
increasing the minimum wage, when Treasury advice is to the contrary?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: The member makes a very interesting point, because the
Treasury advice also recommended a nil increase. We did not accept that advice. In fact,
the Department of Labour’s advice recommen ded a 30c increase. We actually did not
accept that, because we thought a 50c per hour increase was actually fair and reasonable
and sustainable in the circumstances.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: How will she balance the increasing cost of living and low pay for
young people on the minimum wage, when she move d this year to pass legislation to
cut their minimum wage by 20 percent?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Certainly, the question of youth unemployment is an
issue that we are all grappling with. We want  to give employers the incentive to take on
young people, and we want a flexible market regime and a flexible employment regime
that actually encourages bus inesses to get ahead and to take on those young people, so
they get their first foot on that employment ladder.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Will the 50c minimum wage increase address income inequality and
reduce poverty, or was the Minister of M āori Affairs correct when he said “Such a
modest adjustment, from $13 to $13.50, does not reflect the polit ical courage and
strategic vision we need to eliminate poverty”, and is this another example of a growing
rift with the Māori Party?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: In relation to the last por tion of that question, no; but
nobody is saying that this is a s ilver bullet to actua lly address the poverty issue. This is
just one measure, and it is actually interesting when we use the same methodology—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: More like a water pistol than a bullet—more like a water
pistol!

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: —that was used in 2002 by th e then Minister, Margaret
Wilson—and what I would like to ask of the me mber who interjected is, why is it that
when Labour has an increase in line with wage growth, it is a fairer deal—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Ministers do not ask other members questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek leave to table
the confidence and supply agreement of 2005 between the New Zealand First Party and
Labour, which put the minimum wage up from $9 an hour to $12 an hour.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will now resume his seat. That agreement is public
knowledge, and we do not need to waste time tabling such documents.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Pita Sharples
items.text: When will the Minister come to the realisation that an extra
$16.50 a week, which is the after-tax increas e for a person working 40 hours a week on
a minimum wage, will not reverse the dark  plight of children who are living in
minimum wage households, and that if she raised the minimum wage to $16 per hour,
262 Questions for Oral Answer 9 Feb 2012
which is the M āori Party’s policy, $99 per week would go to those wh ānau, who really
need it?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Can I say that I do share the honourable member’s
concern about children in low-income households . It is an important issue, and one that
we discussed during the minimum wage consultation. But, as I have said, increasing the
minimum wage is no silver bullet. The Govern ment is assisting low-income workers in
a number of ways, including through scheme s such as Working for Families. We are
determined to create the right environment to encourage businesses to grow and create
more jobs, rather than legislate an unsust ainable and arbitrary minimum wage level and
risk the loss of significant jobs.
Interest Rates and Lending Practices—Establishment of Helpline
8. PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Consumer Affairs
items.text: What recent announcements has the Government made on
protecting consumers from loan sharks?

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: This week the
Government announced a new freephone number to help protect consumers from being
preyed on by unscrupulous loan companies.  The number, 0800 LOAN STRESS, will
give consumers better access to services to help them understand their rights and resolve
disputes from finance companies. This will empower people to seek protection when
they believe they are getting a raw deal.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What else is the Government  doing to prevent loan sharks
from preying on vulnerable people?

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: The Government will reform consumer credit laws to
better protect consumers. This will include  preventing essential household items from
being used as security for loans, and cr eating a code of res ponsible lending. Draft
legislation will be released in March, and I will be holding a range of meetings across
the country to discuss the issues involved.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What is the Government doing to target unregistered loan
providers?

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: All financial service providers are currently required to be
registered with a dispute resolution servi ce. Unregistered lenders will be targeted
through new provisions in the consumer credit law. One of the proposed changes is that
if a lender is not registered, the consumer will not be required to pay any of the costs of
borrowing. The 0800 LOAN STRESS service will al so assist consumers in finding out
whether their loan provider is registered, a nd which dispute resolution service they are
registered with.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is the first time that
I have ever seen this occur in all my time in Parliament, where a question has been put
down in the name of a member, has been circ ulated in the name of a member—in this
case Jonathan Young—but between the publicati on of the questions and the time of the
House, it has been changed. I know of no precedent, and no ability to make that change.
You are allowed to change th e Minister who answers it, bu t in the past it has always
been done “on behalf of”, after circulation.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not aware of circulation bei ng any particular cut-off time for

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Mr Speaker, may I begin my contribution to
the Address in Reply by congratulating you on your reappointment to the role of
Speaker, and may I also take the opportunity to congratulate the other presiding officers.
Effectively, at the election there were two propositions that voters could vote on.
National’s proposition was to return the Crow n accounts to surplus by 2014; to ensure
that the Government developed good quality public services and to cap the size of those
public services; to do its utmost in rebuilding our second-largest city, Christchurch City,
after those severe earthquakes; and to ma ke available to the public a minority
shareholding of four State- owned enterprises—Mighty River Power, Genesis, Meridian
Energy, and Solid Energy—and also to reduce the Government’s shareholding in Air
New Zealand.
Labour’s proposition was to introduce a capital gains tax of 15 percent, raise the top
tax rate, and borrow more money from ove rseas banks, and—yes—pay the in-work tax
9 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 267
credit to those not working. The Greens we re very similar. They were going to
introduce a capital gains tax at the marginal tax rate, which would have been in the 20-
plus percent range, as we see it. As a result,  it is plain to see that the voters of New
Zealand supported National, giving it 47.3 pe rcent of the party vote, and returning 59
members of Parliament. Together with a solid support from the ACT Party and United
Future, National under the leadership of John Key has formed the Government—an
outstanding result in anyone’s definition. In fact, it is the best percentage party vote ever
in the environment of MMP.

items.speaker: One could ask the question
items.text: “Why was that?”. The answer is simple. It is because the
policies National canvassed with the public during the election made sense to the
public. The policies that Nati onal canvassed with the public  during the election made
sense with the public.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. Could I just say to member s that it is a longstanding convention in
this House that members should not conduct conversations unless it is necessary to do
so, and then only so as not to disrupt pro ceedings. They should show some courtesy to
the member who is trying to address the business of the House.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: At the conclusion of 2011 the Governor-General gave the Speech
from the Throne, which articulated that  work programme of the National-led
Government for the next 3 years. As expected, it was based on those four aims: return
the Crown accounts to surplus by 2014-15, deliv er high-quality public services, rebuild
Christchurch, and offer the public those minor ity shareholdings of the four State-owned
enterprises, as well as reducing the Gove rnment’s shareholding in Air New Zealand.
The largest-ever percentage of New Zealanders voted in favour of those policies.
In the electorate of Kaik ōura we achieved also that best -ever share of the party vote,
and I would like to make the point again of  asking the question why. Well, it is very
simple. It is because under a National-led Government in Marlborough one gets to keep
more of what one earns. In Marlborough, Kaik ōura, and North Canterbury, if we send
more money to Wellington, we never see it again. This means less investment, less
growth, and no jobs for our youth.
National is determined to address those di fficult issues, and in  Marlborough we are
putting together a strategy that has the dual aims of removing the roadblocks to
economic growth and creating enduring job prospects for our youth. At this moment we
have King Salmon going through the Environm ental Protection Auth ority process. It
has done the science, it understands what needs to be done to have a successful
operation in aquaculture, and we look forw ard to it coming through the Environmental
Protection Authority process, whatever the outcome is. If it is successful, that represents
200 jobs in Marlborough.
In terms of infrastructure and energy, Tr ustPower has a proj ect in Marlborough
already consented but still not yet started. That again repres ents another 100 jobs in
Marlborough. In aviation, we have Safe Air in Marlboroug h; we also have the C130
programme. That too potentially can contribut e another 50 jobs into the future. From
those three opportunities that pr esent themselves, there is al so the enlargement of the
contribution of the manufacturing services—a nother 50 jobs. Forestry needs to double
its ability to process forestry and timber; th at represents another 50 jobs. And with the
ongoing upskilling of our workforce in Marlborough, the NMIT—the Nelson
Marlborough Institute of Technology—also can build anot her 20 jobs. So if we can
progress the agenda of this Government, my electorate looks to gain 500 jobs, and that
is what we need to really ensure that there is a place and a career in  this country for our
young folks.
268 Address in Reply 9 Feb 2012
To those who are objectors to economic  growth, I would say: “Show me your
alternatives.” Show me your  alternatives for youth employment, your vision for
Marlborough, and, for that matter, your vi sion for New Zealand. Too many people for
too long in this country have limited th e potential of the provi nces and rural New
Zealand, and that is why, since 2004, this country’s tradable sector has shrunk
dramatically. Labour’s dislike of the rural se ctor is well known, and its regular attacks
on the rural sector before and during the elec tion were obvious for all to see. Is it any
wonder that when one looks at a map today, after the 2011 el ection, it is entirely blue
with regard to provincial rural New Zealand in the party vote situ ation? Why? Because
National is committed to the economy. It is not a tax, borrow, and spend Government.
In this term the National-led Government will continue its agenda to address those
issues that New Zealanders care about. I wi ll make that point again. The National-led
Government will continue its ag enda to address those issues that New Zealanders care
about—issues such as better ed ucation for our youth, starting  with a goal of 98 percent
of all children accessing early childhood education before they start primary school, and
identifying and supporting those youth who need support around literacy and numeracy.
Without that essential support, we are committing them to failure. May I take this
opportunity to pay tribute to  the Ministers Anne Tolley and Hekia Parata for the
wonderful work that they are doing and have done.
National will continue to unclog the health system from its managerialism, or its
over-managerialism, ensuring that money reac hes the doctors and nurses so that they
can perform their miraculous procedures and add to the quality of people’s lives. Today
our hospitals are performing 20,000 more elec tive procedures than they were under the
last Labour administration, and what is more, National’s goal is to  increase the number
by at least 4,000 further elective procedures. Has the Mini ster of Health, Tony Ryall,
not done a great job?
National will continue to take the lead and bring along the publ ic in developing
better ways of preventing child abuse. An outstanding example of this is the present
Green Paper for Vulnerable Children, which is being conducted by the Minister for
Social Development, Paula Bennett. What a great job Minister Paula Bennett is doing in
this area.
National made significant progress in reducing crime during its first term in
Government by increasing the number of uniformed police and equipping them with the
tools to do their job better. We look forw ard with confidence as Minister Collins
continues the outstanding work started by th e previous Minister, Simon Power, in the
law and order area.
That is but a flavour of the work streams that this hard-working Government has as
its programme for the next 3 years. I am sure that my fellow colleagues will articulate
the many other work streams that this Government has to address going forward in their
presentations to the House. In conclusion, New Zealanders can have confidence and
trust that this National-led G overnment will do its level be st—it will do its level best—
for all those who are prepared to help themselves. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Firstly, could I c ongratulate, obviously,
Lockwood Smith, the Speaker, on his reappoint ment. I also pay my respects to the
Governor-General, as is the tradition in this debate.
We are some 2½ months from the last el ection and, oh, how the world has certainly
changed in a number of ways, both globally and domestically. It is interesting how
personalities change and how the cracks in Governments start to open. It is 2½ months
after an election, and I congr atulate the National Party on its substa ntial victory. You
would have thought that unity would have br oken out in this country, peace would have
reigned, and we would now be inheriting the sort of bri ghter future that John Key
9 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 269
promised us not just in one election but in two elections. But if you look at the analysis
over the last months, weeks, and days, what  do we have? We have division in New
Zealand. We have protest. We have cour t action against the Government. We have
Waitangi Tribunal claims being lodged. We have people being insulted—leaders in our
community. We have public discontent. And we have no political leadership and no
ideas from the Government, as evidenced by the Address in Reply debate.
You can tell, of course, when a Government gets arrogant. You can tell when, in the
second term, the Government starts to get a rrogant. Normally it takes a few years of the
second term, but it has taken 2½ months. Yest erday we had the se nior Minister, the
politician of the year, Gerry Brownlee, blow a fuse, a sort of political version of a
blunderbuss, at the Mayor of Christchurch, who I would have thought had got a fair bit
on his plate—as Mr Brownlee doe s every day, of course; thr ee times I think. He called
Bob Parker a clown.
I have to say I sat there for a minute, knowing Mr Brownlee as I do, and tried to
work out where he was at the time when he thought of this wonderful term “clown”.
What sort of inspiration was he thinki ng of? Then it became clear; I looked up
Wikipedia and it became clear. Mr Brownlee’ s favourite restaurant, of course, being
McDonald’s, I thought that must  be his inspiration—the Mc Donald’s clown. Of course
it was, because if you look at Wikipedia, you see that it says about Ronald McDonald,
the clown that represents the fast-food chain, that he “inhabits a fantasy world called
McDonaldland, and has adventures with his friend Mayor McCheese …”. I thought that
must be Gerry; after the third double-meat burger and chips, he blows a fuse and attacks
the Mayor of Christchurch. You know when  a Government is cracking and you know a
Government is starting to get arrogant when you have that sort of stuff going on.
We have protest in this country now, we ha ve division in this country now, and I am
waiting and New Zealand is waiting for the so- called economic brighter future that Mr
Key promised us. If you look at the job figures, of course, you see that full-time jobs are
down, the number of hours worked is down, 100,000 people want or need more hours to
make ends meet, 83,000 people—mostly young pe ople—are not in edu cation, work, or
training, quality jobs are going out the door, and families cannot make ends meet. This
Government’s answer, its only idea—apart from abusing mayors of Christchurch and
others—its only strategy, is, fi rst, just manage and spin the economic decline, manage
the decline, manage the drift south, and, secondly, the big id ea, which of course is not
original, sell State assets. Again, you can tell a Government is cracking when you see
the arrogance come out again.
This Government won an election—I accept that. But I say this: those members
know, and the polls show, that the State-owned en terprise sales, the fire sales that this
Government is going to engage in, have been rejected by New Zealanders, and the
discontent is growing. The thing that Mr Br ownlee does not get, as he blows another
powder keg and has another crac k at people, is that people  in the communities are not
silly and they can work out basic economics . They know, of course, that when you sell
revenue-generating assets, wh en you max the credit card out as this crowd has,
borrowing hundreds of millions of bucks a wee k, when you spend all the cash, as this
crowd has—just like a household spending all its income; all the cash is gone, and you
keep borrowing—your only alternative is to sell something. So you sell the car, but you
keep borrowing on the credit card. So you pa y off maybe a month’s debt, but you keep
borrowing, and on it goes. What do you do th en? You sell the motorbike maybe. You
sell the fridge. You keep selling and you erode your assets.
Well, the communities have worked it out. Mr Brownlee once said on radio that the
communities do not understand budgets, people do not understand basic economics—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I never said that!
270 Address in Reply 9 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Yes, you did, on Newstalk ZB. I say to Mr
Brownlee that if you can balance your house hold budget in these recessionary times,
you would have a PhD in economics, something Mr Brownlee will not even get close
to. People have worked it out. So the Government strategy and the big idea is for this
crowd to sell revenu e-generating assets , and then try to—[ Interruption] Old
“Twinkletoes” at the back is getting fired up.  Then they try to sell it to the people of
New Zealand by saying “We are going to buy schools. We are going to build schools
and the odd bridge. We are going to invest th is money in other a ssets.” People think,
hey, that is not a bad idea—because we are all in favour of schools and better roads and
those things. But here is the difficulty ec onomically: you sell revenue-generating assets,
you forgo the dividends, you buy non - revenue-gen erating assets, and at some point in
time—I know that this will be a bit difficult for Mr Brownlee; use all your fingers and
toes, Gerry—you run out of cash.
Then the proposition is what you do then. You have continued to borrow, you have
no cash, you have sold the asset, you have us ed up the cash, so wh at is the proposition
then? The only option for this Government is to sell more—to sell more. Those
members have this sort of ideological bl ock. Labour members engaged in this in the
1980s—remember, colleagues? But we learnt. These guys engaged in  it in the 1990s,
got re-elected, and did not learn. I invite them to walk down their streets and ask people:
“Are you in favour of selling State-owned enterprises? Are you in favour of selling your
power companies?”. Because people have al so worked out that these are commercial
operations and they know there will be overs eas interest in them. Tony Ryall confirmed
in the House that he has no plans, no ideas, and cannot stop the passing on and onsale of
shares from maybe the odd mum and dad Kiwi who might find some cash, after they
have paid all their household bills—if th ey have got a job—to whip down to the
stockbroker and buy some shares. Government  members have no plans, no options, and
cannot stop shares passing on to overseas interests.
Why would overseas interests—or anybody—buy a State-owned enterprise? They do
not do it out of a charitable spirit. They  buy it to make money. We know what will
happen to power prices. Overseas interests are not going to sit there and say to the
Government they are happy just to take a stat ic dividend or they are happy just to take
less. They are going to say “We want more mo ney.”, and they are go ing to screw it out
of the people of New Zealand.  Peter Dunne will be here somewhere, I am sure; I am
sure I can see him. If the M āori Party acquiesces and actua lly does the right thing and
walks, he may go down in history as this country’s best auctioneer—going, going, gone.
He may well hold the pivotal vote that can e ither stop this going forward or allow it to
go forward. I invite Peter Dunne to reflect on that. He will make history, one way or the
other. He will make history over this.
So the big idea, after you have maxed the card out and got rid of all the cash, is to
flog off the family silver. At least Government members are honest enough to say that if
they win another election, they will consider doing it again, but they will do it after the
election. So we know that once they have so ld these assets, there are others on the
block. There is a campaign being engendere d and generated around the country from
grassroots Kiwis who have been down this ro ad before, do not like it , know that it does
not work, and know that this crowd are bereft of ideas. We can tell they are bereft of
ideas because they start attacking good, comm unity folk. When you attack in the press
the Mayor of Christchurch, who has probably got the hardest job in New Zealand as a
mayor, trying to rebuild his city, because you blew a fuse—maybe you did not have a
decent kip the night before, or the tuck s hop was closed before you got there—it is a
sign of a Government under stress.
9 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 271
It is going to be interesting, as we go th rough this State-owned enterprises debate, to
see the twisting and the turning that will occu r over section 9. It is happening now. The
Prime Minister knows the complications in respect of the creative remedies around that.
But I invite the next speake r to get up and explain Mr Br ownlee’s actions, and I invite
the Government to think very carefully. Mr Brownlee’s actions are an example of where
it is heading.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: One of this nation’s finest leaders said of
leadership that “Having a vision is not enough. Change comes through … turning [a
vision] into a reality. It is easy to espous e worthy goals, values and polices; the hard
part is implementation.” Tragically, 10 years ago the architec t of those words, Sir Peter
Blake, lost his life in the pursuit of turnin g his vision into a reality. The essence of the
Blake ethos centred around the notion that it is your actions  that define you, not your
words—something that can be easily forgotten by those well intentioned in their pursuit
of public service. I raise th is because in 2008, as a recipient of a Sir Peter Blake
leadership award, I had cause to reflect on my journey, the importance of leadership,
and the visions that I wanted to see become realities. That moment was a turning point
and much of the reason I am here today, something I will expand on shortly.
But, firstly, Mr Speaker, I acknowledge you for your re-nomination, and for the
dignity and decorum you bring to this role . Can I acknowledge the Prime Minister and
Ministers of the Crown for the tremendous so cial and economic leadership that you
have and will continue to show this nati on, and express how humble and privileged I
feel to become part of this National ca ucus team, working to serve the positive
aspirations of all New Zealanders. Can I al so acknowledge our part y president, Peter
Goodfellow, the National Party board he leads, and the team  from the service centre. I
want to sincerely thank you all for the assistance you have provided me, and
acknowledge the outstanding leadership and support you provide our party. In particular
can I thank Grant McCallum, who is also my campaign chair. I also pay tribute to the
electorate team in Northland. Our success in the election is just that—our success.
Nothing could have been achieved without you, and although I am the net result of
those efforts in my election as  MP, I want you to know that th is has and always will be
a team effort. I want to especially make mention of Sally Macauley, our electorate chair,
the longest serving in the party; Neil Clemen ts, my deputy chair, a very wise political
gentleman; Ross Miller, a loyal and guiding hand; and a specia l thanks to the evergreen
June Levet, the “Mrs National Party” of the north.
At this stage I would also like to pay tri bute to my predecessor, the Hon John Carter,
for the massive contribution he made to this  party, to Northland, and to this nation. Of
course, “massive contribution” could also desc ribe the tab he now ha s at Trader Jacks,
but I am sure the Cooks will be well serv ed with him as their high commissioner, not
only for the passion he brings to make a diffe rence but also for the range of new jokes
he will be unleashing on an unsuspecting popul ation. I want to offer my thanks to all
Northlanders who supported me through the campaign and have trusted in me to be
their representative. I owe you all a debt of gratitude, and I hope to repay this in kind by
being as effective as I can be as your MP in representing the hopes and positive
aspirations of Northland and our region.
Lastly, I want to thank my family—my wond erful parents, siblings, and children. I
am who I am because of you, and I could not be more proud to be part of the family that
we are. Also I make a special thanks to my partner Sandra. I have not always been lucky
in love, but my Powerball number certainly came up in that particular lottery, when
Sandra came into my life. Thank you very muc h, Sandra, for sharing my life with me in
the way you do.
272 Address in Reply 9 Feb 2012
I would now like to share with you three im portant themes: who I am, what I believe
in, and why I am here. I am the eldest s on of Lew and Merlene Sabin, and I have one
brother and sister. I am the proud father  of three amazing children—as you can see,
these family things do get to me, Mr Speaker—Brook, Darryl, and Brenna. I am of
mixed genealogy like most, and I am proudl y of Tainui whakapapa on my mother’s
side. It gives me a uniqueness in this worl d, and I celebrate that. But I celebrate more
that I am a New Zealander and I call this place my home.
My early years were spent in Auckland befo re we as a family moved to Whangarei,
and I am a product of Whangarei Boys Hi gh School. I left school and followed my
father’s footsteps into the navy as a seaman officer, but before long I found myself back
in Northland, dairy farming. However, as a young father I was keen to join the police,
essentially to contribute to making the community I was bringing my children up in a
better place. With that in mind my policing career was soon focused in the area of drug
enforcement, primarily because I felt that th e best way to make a difference was to get
to the cause of the problem. One quickly co mes to the conclusion in that particular
vocation that alcohol and drug abuse is the cause more often than not.
My career in the police shadowed the in troduction of pure methamphetamine, or P,
into New Zealand—an area I have develope d an expertise in—but while working on
squads running undercover on  electronic surveillance opera tions, I literally saw New
Zealand explode from having no P problem to the worst in the world within 5 years.
Our well-developed drug culture saw us primed for the only hard drug in the world that
you can make on your kitchen bench from read ily available retail chemicals. Those 5
years have changed New Zealand for ever, and led me to the conclusion that the fight
needed to go back to the top of the cliff. Quite simply, I came to the conclusion that we
would not win the war trying to heal the wounded.
This desire to find a better way gave ri se to Methcon Group, a drug-education and
policy company I founded in 2006 and opera ted from then. The mission was simple:
empower employees, students, and the commun ity with education, while working to
find policy solutions to help provide the Gove rnment with better t ools. It was a long,
difficult, and often lonely journey and one that many told me was futile, and one that
many told me was someone else’s problem to  fix. Nevertheless I stuck to the task at
hand, the primary reason being that I just believed that someone needed to do
something. Could I at this time pay tribut e to the Prime Minister and acknowledge the
outstanding leadership on this particular issue. It has indeed been a gamebreaker.
That challenge was put into chilling c ontext, however, when on Anzac Day 2009 my
fight went from P to that of my son’s surv ival, when he suffered a catastrophic bleed on
the brain during a game of rugby. This could get tough, Mr Sp eaker. Following his
emergency surgery, I was confronted with the news that his death was imminent,
something I refused to accept, as well as the contention that if he did survive, it would
likely be in a vegetative state. Like his old man, my boy is a fighter. I knew that, even if
they did not. I pledged to fight with him to help get his life back. It was a frightening
journey, full of heartache, but one in whic h we never lost hope. Sometimes hope is the
only thing you have to cling to. When that is the case you just have to develop an iron
grip. Something I am very proud to say is that  we have been rewarded today, as my son
sits in the gallery larg er than life, fit and healthy, to  watch proceedings. That taught me
that it is not what happens in  life that defines y ou, it is what you do about it. It was a
difficult couple of years, but by now my goa l was to enter politics, and I sold my
business to allow for a full-time campaign in an endeavour to try to win the selection
and the election that followed.
While there are some who would say that I am a one-trick pony here to further the
anti-drug cause, far from it: my journey into politics has come about as an evolution of
9 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 273
many professional and life experiences, leadi ng me to the simple conclusion that if one
wants to support their community in achieving its  real potential, there is a need for one
to be around the table where the decisions that are most affecting your communities are
being made. The reality is, my efforts on the P issue demonstrate more my willingness
to try to make a difference than my focus on that one issue alone. Much like my son, I
just wanted to try to find solutions, while many others were finding ways to tolerate the
symptoms.
I would now like to share with you a little bit of what I believe in. I am a proud
representative of the New Zealand National Party because its founding values resonate
with who I am as an individua l. Central to this  is personal responsibility, reward for
hard work and enterprise, limited govern ment, and equality of opportunity and
citizenship. It is a fast-paced  world we live in and much has changed, even in my
lifetime, with regard to the fabric that binds the society together and the balance
required to maintain a healthy, socio-econom ic equilibrium. Too often, in my view, a
sense of pride, self-reliance, and indepe ndence is usurped by cultural entitlement,
despite the implicit irony that so many wh o contribute nothing to society have
developed an almost self-righteous belief that society owes them something. Striving to
succeed and success itself are so often frowned upon as threatening and somehow
discriminating against those who seek re fuge behind the ever-growing veil of
mediocrity. Participation, it seems, is now the goal, and winning, as an equal part,
unnecessary and intimidatory. Personal respons ibility, the very source from which self-
respect itself springs, is intrinsically relate d to the individual’s willingness to accept
responsibility over one’s life. To  do so is to give value, purpose, and freedom to the
soul; to refuse it leaves a hole from which the spirit of the individual will slowly but
surely drain.
Yet years of socialist ideology, welfarism, which has evolved to provide perverse
incentives to opt out, and the insidious encroachment of Government into the minds and
lives of citizens have seen the notion of pe rsonal responsibility pill oried like it was the
ramblings of capitalist zealots. This c ountry is God’s own, yet we condemn many
children to child abuse, neglec t, and homicide. For a genera tion we have vainly sought
solutions, largely ignoring the fact that what we  have created is a culture in which it is
too easy for parents to become trapped in we lfare, often through no fault of their own,
who lack even the most basic of life skills , and for whom personal responsibility is an
unnecessary and irrelevant commodity, surpasse d by the sea of social agencies that will
now seek to provide what they will never have to. Too often we have become consumed
with addressing the symptoms of these very problems, while  failing to challenge the
cause of them, something that often requi res courage and honesty in uncomfortable
amounts, but none the less something, in my view, that New Zealand expects of its
leaders. To that end I would like to co mmend the work being done by the Minister for
Social Development in this particular area.  The long and short of it is a little bit of
personal responsibility will go a long way, but the lack thereof will go a lot further—
just in the wrong direction.
And why am I here? I am a great believer that a marriage of quality education and
equality of opportunity are the essential building blocks of so cial well-being and
prosperity. I am here because I want to do all I can to ensure that this environment
exists to help Northland and New Zealand reach the obvious potential that we hold. I
also come here with a focus to see Northl and develop a whole-of-region economic plan
that clearly outlines a path to reaching that potential, the barriers that may stand in the
way, and the opportunities we have to make our boat go faster. And there are many. Too
often Northland is singled out for all the wrong reasons, but let me make it quite clear to
you today, these less-than-flatte ring statistics are not the failure; our failure is that
274 Address in Reply 9 Feb 2012
Northland is blessed with economic potential  but we have no plan to achieve it—not
yet, anyway. On that note can I suggest th at if any members of the House are looking
for some good beachside property in Northland, then it may pay to get in quick!
The last point I want to make relates to judgment. As elected representatives, one of
our primary roles, in my view, is the exer cise of judgment. Edm und Burke, viewed by
many as a philosophical f ounder of modern conservatism, said of judgment: “Your
representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays, instead
of serving you, if he sacrifi ces it to your opinion.” In a wo rld that is over-managed and
under-led, leadership and judgm ent are what New Zealanders need and expect of us—
something I will always keep top-of-mind.
So in conclusion, who am I? I am a proud fath er of a blended family of six, richer in
spirit for the good and bad experiences of my  personal life, poorer, financially, for the
fact that I have managed to amass six children somehow in the process. I am a
passionate Northlander. I am  passionate about Northla nd and New Zealand, and the
pursuit of the potential therein. What do I believe in? That personal responsibility is just
that: the responsibility of the person, not the Government; th at carrots work better than
sticks, but that both are necessary; that the first question we should be asking New
Zealanders is “What is your dream?”, and th en set about creating a social and economic
environment to help make those dreams po ssible. Why am I here? I am here for the
implementation. Quite simply, I want to help turn visions into realities. Thank you.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: I move, That the debate
